headline: Super Mario 64 ported to Microsoft Zune HD, running natively on the 2009 media player
summary: The classic Nintendo 64 game now runs natively on the Zune HD, a 2009-era device, playing mostly at full speed with sound and touch controls thanks to its Nvidia Tegra hardware and OpenZDK.
details: The classic Nintendo 64 game Super Mario 64 has been successfully ported to the Microsoft Zune HD, running natively on the device's hardware. This unofficial project, built using the OpenZDK kit, plays mostly at full speed with sound and touch controls. It leverages the Zune HD's Nvidia Tegra APX 2600 chip.

Released in 2009, the Zune HD was Microsoft's answer to Apple's iPod, featuring a 3.3-inch OLED touchscreen. Originally priced between $219.99 and $289.99, Microsoft halted its production in 2011, but an exploit later enabled homebrew development via OpenZDK.

The port relies on native ARM code running atop the Zune HD's Windows CE-based OS, without modifying the device's firmware. It utilizes an OpenGL ES 2 renderer with prebuilt shader variants, circumventing the Zune's inability to compile GLSL shaders directly.

Game logic operates at 30 ticks per second, though some lag can occur if the Zune can't keep up. The game renders at 480x272 resolution in landscape mode, with audio processing on a separate, higher-priority thread to maintain quality. A customizable touchscreen overlay provides all necessary controls.

This project builds upon the 2019 fan-led Super Mario 64 decompilation effort, which provides a C source code. Users must provide a ROM dumped from their own cartridge, with the build process running on Docker in Linux before transferring to the device via USB.

While Nintendo has previously targeted sites hosting unofficial PC ports, this Zune HD version joins a growing list of community ports across various platforms. Notably, the repository's first commit indicates partial assistance from AI, specifically Claude Opus 5.5.

headline: Indie game dev nets $15K/year despite $560K sales
summary: A co-founder of Northend Games revealed that after refunds, Steam fees, taxes, and publisher cuts, his annual take-home pay from two successful titles was just $15,000.
details: Omer Develioğlu, co-founder of Northend Games, shared a candid financial breakdown of his indie studio's success. Despite generating $560,000 in sales for two Steam titles, Northend Tower Defense and Deepstone Rift (Early Access), over five years, the net profit was significantly lower.

The gross sales figure of $560,000 from 135,000 units sold was heavily impacted by a 22% refund rate, particularly from China, which is disproportionately high. This alone accounted for $134,000 in refunds.
Steam's platform fee, which starts at 30% for most developers, took another substantial cut of $127,000. This left the developers with $297,000 before other deductions.

Further deductions included U.S. withholding taxes (5%) and a publisher's cut of $115,000, which covered PR, distribution, and marketing in Asian regions. This publisher fee, potentially around 35-40% of net income, left the take-home amount at $172,000.

After Thailand's local taxes (15%) reduced the amount to $146,000, the remaining sum was split 50/50 with Develioğlu's co-founder. This resulted in a personal total of $73,000 over five years, equating to approximately $15,000 per year.

While this annual income is more than the average wage in Thailand ($5,280), Develioğlu noted that he still drives a 2012 Mazda, a far cry from the riches one might expect from half a million dollars in game sales.
